tasks.title: Build the autonomous no-Blender asset pipeline
tasks.summary: Generated every cel-shift asset autonomously from declarative RON: an 11-bone rigged technician with Idle, Walk and Repair clips, a merged eight-cabinet rack row with server slots and status lights, a cooling unit, the red utility cart and yellow step stool, and overhead tray plus black hose modules.

tasks.title: Load assets and build the data hall
tasks.summary: Loaded every generated GLB through an explicit Loading, Ready, and Failed asset state with no procedural fallback, cached one unit mesh per primitive shape and one unlit material per palette role, and spawned the authored 40 m square hall: a polished floor inside low perimeter walls, four rack rows separated by three traversable aisles, four cooling units, three overhead trays with hose drops, painted yellow aisle and walkway markings, the red service cart, and the yellow step stool. Visual and collider lists stay separate and are joined by stable PropId, the colliders are extracted once into a cached vector, and a room-wide flood fill proves every aisle checkpoint shares one walkable component with the player spawn.

tasks.title: Add the rigged technician and real keyboard movement
tasks.summary: Spawned the generated 11-bone technician only after the assets and the hall were both ready, bound every required rig node into explicit PlayerParts with the rest transform captured before any clip played, and moved it from the real ButtonInput<KeyCode> arrow state. A public ViewBasis resource, initialised to the reviewed NorthEast 45-degree view, is the only screen-to-world interface movement reads, so the orbit task becomes its runtime updater without changing a movement rule. Opposite arrows cancel and diagonals are normalized, world X and world Z resolve separately against the cached colliders and radius-aware room bounds so the technician slides along rack faces, and facing plus the Idle and Walk clips follow the accepted displacement rather than the request. The idle transition stops Walk, explicitly restores every PlayerParts rest transform, and only then plays Idle; the Repair clip is bound for the operations task and nothing plays it yet. Missing, duplicate, and stale rig nodes are typed failures that stop movement instead of being silently skipped.

tasks.title: Add clamped four-way camera orbit
tasks.summary: Spawned the one orthographic game camera with the reviewed fixed 26 m by 14.625 m rectangle, 57-degree elevation, zero roll, and the initial NorthEast 45-degree yaw, which is all the authored unlit hall needs to be visible. Real Q and E just_pressed frames retarget the desired heading immediately, opposite keys on one frame cancel exactly, and the yaw eases with smoothstep at a constant 90 degrees per 0.30 seconds, so a retarget mid-tween starts at the interpolated yaw and its duration scales with the shortest remaining angle instead of restarting a fixed clock. CameraPlugin is now the sole runtime updater of ViewBasis and publishes the live interpolated basis in UpdateOrbitIntent, before MovePlayer reads it, so the technician walks along the camera it can actually see mid-orbit. Every frame the ground quadrilateral is cast from the current yaw, its axis-aligned extents are subtracted from the active blueprint's own room.coverage, and the followed technician is clamped into what remains before the transform is derived, so an overridden hall is followed by the coverage it declares rather than by the authored constant. The walkable room stays exactly 40 m, but the camera is clamped against the rendered coverage the new visual apron fills, so it overhangs the room freely and follows every legal player position exactly: every room corner is centred with the full 360 px of margin at every heading and at every exact tween midpoint, while the whole view stays inside the apron and zoom, elevation, and roll stay fixed. Framing is measured against the technician's whole generated spatial envelope rather than its ground origin -- the rest pose and every sampled Idle, Walk, and Repair pose, cel outlines included, 0.7998 m of radius and a 1.9704 m crown -- and every corner of it keeps at least 32 logical pixels of viewport margin, calibrated against an independent 49.23077 px per metre edge point.

tasks.title: Add recurring faults, prioritized tickets, and repair
tasks.summary: Attached the documented rack state machine to the four authored rack-row HallProp entities by stable PropId, joined to their cached collider rectangles once, and drove it from one seeded ChaCha8 fault stream. The scheduler is a pure sequence generator: every four simulated seconds an opportunity matures and the timer stops accumulating, a full queue pauses it without consuming a single word of randomness, and a drawn candidate whose rack already holds a ticket or is still resolving or cooling down is held rather than rerolled, so the exact rack and severity order is the same whatever the player does and only its timing moves. Tickets carry stable monotonic identifiers and sort Critical before Warning, then by creation tick, then by rack; the queue enforces the maximum of three active tickets and one ticket per rack and reports which rack it refused. A real Space press gathers only open faults, measures distance to each rack's collider rectangle rather than its centre, and selects by severity, then distance, then creation tick, then rack, so an out-of-range press changes nothing and is recorded as a named rejection instead of a silent no-op. Starting a repair in UpdateOperations locks movement in the same frame, before MovePlayer runs, zeroes the published motion, plays the generated Repair clip, and exposes the blue wrench state for the HUD task while the camera keeps orbiting and following. Repair completes on its own after three seconds and releases the lock, the healthy indicator shows for two seconds, the ticket then leaves the queue as the rack begins an eight second cooldown, and only a fully recovered rack is eligible again.

tasks.title: Add operations HUD and diegetic badges
tasks.summary: Added src/hud.rs, which draws the whole operations HUD from the live operations model and owns no gameplay state of its own: every frame it reads TicketQueue, RackOperations, RackRoster, MovementLock, LastInteraction, and the real camera, and writes only presentation components plus one observable HudReport, so there is no second ticket model to drift. The top-left stack renders up to three rows straight out of the queue's own global priority order rather than re-sorting it, each row carrying a severity chip, a rack-state chip, a short real label such as T0002 R01 Critical, and a dwell-progress bar; shape carries meaning beside colour, with a square critical chip against a round warning chip and sharp, rounded, and pill badges for fault, repair, and resolved. The status line is derived from live state alone, preferring a running repair, then a real out-of-range rejection while that rejection is still true of the one rack it named, then the queue; move_closer_still_stands re-reads the live queue, that rack's live state, its roster collider, and the technician's live position every frame, so the prompt clears the moment that rack's ticket leaves the queue, that rack stops being Faulted, or the technician walks inside repair range, and another rack's open ticket can never keep a stale prompt alive. Badges are fixed-size screen-space UI nodes anchored every frame from a stable world point 2.4 m above each rack's collider centre through the real Camera::world_to_viewport, reading the camera's own Transform rather than its propagated GlobalTransform so they never lag a tween by a frame, a substitution the camera query enforces with Without<ChildOf> so a parented camera is refused as unusable and its badges are hidden rather than projected through a local transform pretending to be a global one; a visible anchor always gets a fully visible badge because the badge box is clamped inside the viewport and its thin leader line is rotated to end exactly on the projected anchor, while an anchor that leaves the viewport hides explicitly and a refused projection is recorded as a typed error. The bottom-right strip names Arrows, Q, E, and Space and shows which are live, turning the Space cap hard-hat blue and flattening the Arrows cap while a repair holds the technician still. Every colour is a typed PaletteRole, the 216 px queue stack and 40 px control strip keep a 16 px margin and stay outside the central 50% x 50% play rectangle at both 1280x720 and 960x540, and HudReport reports a rack that lost its RackOperations, a ticket whose rack is unknown, a missing row node, a missing badge node exactly once rather than once per write and again per hide, an unusable game camera, and a camera with no viewport, each under its own BadgeVisibility variant so no failure is ever explained with another's name. Shape, glyph, and progress are node-level contracts: the app tests read Node::border_radius off the severity chips and off all three badge states, the glyph text off the real RackBadgeLabel node, and the progress bar's Node::width against the live dwell progress, and each is covered by a mutation that fails when the write is deleted or swapped.

challenges.title: Byte-reproducible rigged assets with no external content tool
challenges.impact: The plan forbids Blender, manual export, and human approval, so the rig, animation clips, and merged equipment geometry had to come from repository-owned source that a build gate can regenerate and byte-compare. Any hash-ordered map, embedded timestamp, or unquantized trigonometric value would have made the committed GLBs unverifiable.
challenges.approach: Assets are declared in assets/source/*.ron and tessellated by src/assetgen.rs. Every collection is ordered by declaration order or by the fixed PaletteRole order, every float is quantized onto a 1e-6 grid with negative zero normalised away, and the asset generator string is a constant with no version, host, path, or time data. Static geometry is merged into one primitive per palette role so server slots and LEDs never become runtime entities.
challenges.resolution: assetgen --check regenerates all five assets into two separate temporary roots, requires the two generations to be byte identical, and then requires the committed GLBs to match them exactly. tests/asset_contract.rs additionally parses every output and asserts node and scene names, the 11 named joints, the three clips, rigid skin weights, approved palette materials, finite bounds, valid indices, and the merge and triangle budgets.

challenges.title: Proving real Bevy asset loading and hall identity with no GPU and no fallback
challenges.impact: The reviewed plan forbids any procedural fallback when a generated asset is missing or wrong, but a hall that silently substitutes geometry looks identical to a healthy one in a screenshot. The contract therefore had to be proved inside a real Bevy app, and the verification machine has no GPU adapter, so a normal windowed run could not be the gate.
challenges.approach: src/assets.rs loads every generated document and every declared module scene, polls recursive dependency load state, and additionally requires each loaded glTF document to expose the module scene name the pipeline declares, so a mislabelled but structurally valid file still fails. Failures are recorded in AssetLoadReport and move the app to AssetLoadState::Failed; src/world.rs only spawns on entering AssetLoadState::Ready and refuses to spawn an invalid blueprint at all. Tests drive a real App built from DefaultPlugins with WinitPlugin disabled and RenderPlugin created with no wgpu backend, which registers every asset type and runs the real glTF loader headlessly.
challenges.resolution: tests/app_contract.rs boots that headless app against the committed assets and asserts Ready, exact spawned entity, transform, cached mesh, palette material, and shared scene-handle contracts, then repeats the run against private copies of the assets with one file removed, one file truncated, and one file replaced by a different module, requiring AssetLoadState::Failed, a report naming the offending path, and zero spawned props each time.

challenges.title: Explicit rig handles that fail loudly without breaking on Bevy instance respawn
challenges.impact: The reviewed plan requires explicit named rig handles and an explicit failure when one goes missing, duplicated, or stale, because a movement system that silently skips a bone looks identical to a working one. Bevy despawns and respawns a whole glTF world instance whenever a sub-asset event arrives for the file it came from, so handles captured on the first spawn can be invalidated wholesale through no fault of the game. A binder that only ran once produced an intermittent all-parts-stale failure under parallel test load, and a binder that healed on any change would have silently swallowed the real fault the plan requires it to report.
challenges.approach: The generated technician root shares its name with the glTF scene, so it is deliberately excluded from the rig contract and the spawned entity is the stable handle for the instance; the contract covers the skinned mesh node and the eleven skin joints. One binder runs every frame: it costs twelve name lookups while the bound handles still resolve, and otherwise rescans the spawned instance. A rescan that yields a complete rig is a legal rebind, an empty rescan means the instance is mid-respawn and the bound handles are left untouched, and an incomplete rescan keeps the previously bound handles and reports them as typed StalePart errors. Movement and animation are gated on the report being empty in the same frame, not on a state transition that lands a frame late.
challenges.resolution: tests/app_contract.rs fault-injects the failure by despawning bone-tool inside a running app and requires exactly PlayerRigError::StalePart for that node, PlayerRigState::Failed, and a technician position that does not move again. Pure tests in src/player.rs cover missing and duplicate names directly. The full app contract suite, which builds several real headless Bevy apps in parallel, was run ten consecutive times with no failures after the binder became rescan based instead of change-detection based.

challenges.title: Framing every room corner without ever rendering the void outside the hall
challenges.impact: Task 5 asked for two properties at once: a camera whose ground footprint never leaves the 40 m room, and a technician framed with at least 32 pixels of viewport margin at every room corner, at every heading, and at every tween midpoint. Those cannot both hold. Because the orthographic rectangle is rotated relative to the room, the legal follow rectangle is room bounds minus the rotated footprint's axis-aligned extents, which is strictly smaller than the standard axis-aligned clamp that keeps a followed point exactly on the view edge. A technician standing in a corner fell 12.505 m behind the far ground edge, 516 px off screen, and no room size fixed it because the room cancels out of the algebra: framing a corner would have needed an orthographic width of at most 0.99 m instead of the reviewed 26 m.
challenges.approach: The controller separated the two squares the old rule conflated. The walkable, collidable room stays exactly 40 m with its existing perimeter walls, and nothing about the reviewed projection, elevation, headings, tween, or ViewBasis ordering moved. Beneath and outside it the blueprint now authors a 72 m square non-playable visual apron in the cel-shift floor-shadow role, dropped 0.05 m so the coplanar 40 m floor never z-fights, with no collider and no walkable cells: building shell, not a second room. The camera clamp is now taken against RENDER_COVERAGE_SIZE rather than ROOM_SIZE, so the camera overhangs the room freely and follows every legal player position exactly. 72 m is the smallest whole metre that works: the widest ground overhang is hypot(13, 8.71916) = 15.6532 m, so covering a 20 m room half extent needs 71.3065 m, leaving 0.3468 m of slack at the worst yaw.
challenges.resolution: The impossibility contract was replaced by positive real-app contracts. camera_orbit_frames_every_room_corner_with_the_reviewed_margin drives the running app to all four room corners at all four settled headings and two tween samples each, asserts each tween sample really lies between headings, and requires both the reachable corner and the wall corner itself to keep at least 32 px of margin through Bevy's real Camera::world_to_viewport, with the followed corner centred to within half a pixel and holding the full 360 px half-viewport. camera_orbit_holds_the_rendered_apron_instead_of_leaking_past_it proves the follow target is never clamped at a corner, that the whole ground quadrilateral stays inside the 72 m coverage, and that it genuinely does overhang the 40 m room, so the apron is load bearing rather than decorative. camera_orbit_renders_the_apron_over_every_position_the_camera_can_reach sweeps 720 yaws by every framing sample and pins the 15.6532 m and 71.3065 m closed forms. The blueprint validator replaced the non-empty-interval rule with RoomOutsideCameraCoverage, which rejects any coverage that cannot follow the whole walkable room, and added MissingRenderApron, RenderApronDoesNotCoverRenderedArea, and RenderApronHasCollider so the apron cannot silently shrink, rise into the floor, or gain a collider.

challenges.title: A recurring fault stream whose order the player cannot change
challenges.impact: Task 6 demanded two properties that pull against each other: an exact seeded rack and severity sequence that a test can pin, and a live queue capped at three tickets with no duplicate rack, whose occupancy depends entirely on when the player chooses to walk over and press Space. The obvious scheduler draws a rack every four seconds and rerolls whenever the drawn rack is unavailable, but then the number of words consumed from the stream is a function of player behaviour, so repairing early or late silently produces a different sequence and the pinned expectation becomes untestable.
challenges.approach: The stream was made a pure ordered generator rather than a sampler of the current world. The four second timer arms an opportunity and then stops accumulating, so a pause can never stack two opportunities. Nothing is drawn at all while the queue holds three tickets, and a candidate that has been drawn is held, never discarded: if its rack already holds a ticket, or is still repairing, resolving, or cooling down, the scheduler reports exactly which rack and which state blocked it and waits. Consumption is therefore always two words per candidate and never a function of the player. The seeded RNG is wrapped in a counter so the draw total is observable, and every timer is a std Duration of whole nanoseconds rather than an accumulated f32, so the exact tick boundaries are reproducible.
challenges.resolution: operations_scheduler_sequence_is_independent_of_repair_timing drives the same scheduler through a hostile timeline of irregular repairs and recoveries and requires the emitted pairs to equal the undisturbed sequence exactly. operations_scheduler_consumes_no_randomness_while_the_queue_is_full holds the queue at capacity for ten further seconds and requires zero draws, one recorded pause, and immediate emission on the tick capacity reopens. operations_scheduler_holds_a_drawn_candidate_whose_rack_is_busy proves a held candidate is never rerolled and is released unchanged. In the real app, recurring_ticket_journey runs 2106 fixed sixtieth of a second frames, fills the queue to three simultaneous tickets, completes at least three real Space repairs, and observes two racks fault again after their cooldowns, one of them on the exact tick its eight second cooldown ended, while the opened sequence still matches the pinned seed prefix.

challenges.title: Diegetic rack badges that stay legible through every heading, tween, and resize
challenges.impact: Task 7 asks for badges that float over the racks they belong to while the camera orbits through four headings and tweens between them, and for fixed panels that never cover the middle of the screen at either supported window size. A world-space badge satisfies the first requirement by rotating, shearing, and resizing with the isometric camera, which is exactly what a readable status marker must not do. Anchoring a fixed-size screen-space node instead moves the whole problem into projection, where three failures are silent by default: a rack behind the camera or outside the viewport projects to a meaningless point, a rack near an edge produces a badge that is half off screen, and a camera transform that is one frame stale makes every badge lag visibly through a 0.30 s orbit.
challenges.approach: Badges are Bevy UI nodes of fixed pixel size, anchored every frame from a stable authored world point 2.4 m above each rack collider centre through the real Camera::world_to_viewport. The pass reads the camera entity's own Transform rather than its propagated GlobalTransform, because propagation runs in PostUpdate and the HUD runs in Update after the camera follow; the camera has no parent, so its transform is its global transform and the badge is anchored against this frame's camera rather than last frame's. Off-screen and refused projections are distinct typed outcomes rather than a shared silent skip: an anchor outside the viewport hides as OffScreen, and a ViewportConversionError becomes a typed ProjectionFailure recorded in HudReport. A visible anchor always yields a fully visible badge because the badge box is clamped inside the viewport, and because clamping breaks the vertical relationship between badge and rack, the leader line is a rotated thin node whose local +Y axis is turned onto the direction of the anchor, so it still ends exactly on the rack it names. The fixed panels avoid the central play rectangle on one axis each: the queue stack is 216 px wide, narrower than a quarter of the 960 px verification viewport, and the control strip is 40 px tall, shorter than a quarter of its 540 px height.
challenges.resolution: operations_hud_badges_track_the_projected_rack_at_every_heading_and_mid_tween sweeps all four headings and one genuine mid-tween frame at each, and requires every badge's recorded anchor to equal the test's own independent projection of the same world point, its visibility to agree with whether that projection is on screen, its laid-out ComputedNode to stay exactly 34x22 px and fully inside the viewport, and its leader line to end within 1.5 px of the anchor. operations_hud_clamps_an_edge_badge_and_still_points_its_leader_at_the_rack walks the technician until a faulted rack is pushed against a side edge, the only case where the leader is not vertical, and proves the clamped badge stays on screen while the tilted leader still ends on the rack; flipping the sign of the leader rotation fails only this contract. operations_hud_panels_stay_on_screen_and_clear_of_the_play_rectangle resizes the real window to 1280x720 and 960x540 through a real WindowResized message and re-checks the 16 px margins, the row order, the panel containment, and the play rectangle at both sizes. operations_hud_hides_a_badge_whose_rack_leaves_the_viewport, operations_hud_reports_a_rack_that_lost_its_operational_state, and operations_hud_reports_a_missing_camera_instead_of_drawing_stale_badges cover the three hiding paths, two of them fault-injected into a running app and required to name a typed HudError.

challenges.title: Proving a real rendered browser frame without npm, Selenium, or a GPU
challenges.impact: The reviewed plan forbids npm and any browser automation package, so nothing off the shelf could drive Chrome. A gate that only waited for a load event, or only screenshotted a page, would pass on a blank canvas, on a game that threw during initialization, and on a build whose WebGL context never produced a frame. The two obvious readiness signals are also both unreliable on their own: a Bevy app reaches its first Update long before the hall, rig, roster, and HUD exist, and a canvas can carry the right CSS box while rendering nothing.
challenges.approach: Readiness and rendering are proved independently. src/web.rs holds a pure, natively tested handshake model: every production subsystem is mapped onto Pending, Ready, or Failed, a missing camera or viewport stays Pending because it is an unfinished startup frame, and only two consecutive settled PostUpdate frames latch data-game-state="ready". A failure latches data-game-state="error" once and appends a sanitized detail, with absolute paths reduced to file names and the message bounded, so a browser never shows a build host path. scripts/browser_gate.py is a repository-owned Chrome DevTools Protocol client written against the Python standard library, including a hand-rolled RFC 6455 WebSocket frame codec and a minimal PNG decoder, so the gate injects trusted keyboard input and reads real pixels with no third-party package. Chromium runs headless on SwiftShader, so no GPU is required.
challenges.resolution: scripts/web-smoke.sh serves the package below the /midcreek-cs-1/ project prefix on an available loopback port, requires HTTP 200 for every packaged URL, requires data-game-state="ready" within 30 seconds, requires #browser-errors to be empty, requires the canvas to be visible and 16:9 within one pixel, and requires the canvas region of a real screenshot to carry at least three approved palette classes and real channel variance. The no-scroll assertion carries its own positive control: the same trusted Arrow, Q, E, and Space events must scroll the page while the canvas is blurred and must not scroll it while the canvas is focused, so a page that simply could not scroll fails instead of passing. Deleting one generated GLB from a packaged build drives the gate to exit 1 with the sanitized 'assets: generated/rack.glb failed to load' detail, and the healthy package reports ready in about five seconds with five approved palette classes over the full 1152x648 canvas.

challenges.title: Shipping the whole production game as one publishable WebAssembly file
challenges.impact: The Pages site is published by force-pushing a generated pages-live branch, so every published file must clear GitHub's hard 100 MB blob limit. A stock release build of the full Bevy game for wasm32-unknown-unknown produced a 117.7 MB module, which could never have been pushed, and no amount of retrying the deployment would have revealed the real cause.
challenges.approach: The module was measured section by section rather than guessed at: the WebAssembly name section alone was 49.7 MB and the code section was 59.1 MB. wasm-bindgen now runs with --remove-name-section and --remove-producers-section, the release profile uses fat LTO with one codegen unit and panic=abort, and .cargo/config.toml applies -Copt-level=s only to wasm32-unknown-unknown so the native release build keeps its own optimization level. The same file also supplies the getrandom wasm_js backend the browser target requires.
challenges.resolution: The published game_bg.wasm is 34.5 MB, comfortably inside the blob limit, and scripts/build-web.sh refuses to publish a package that is missing any of index.html, play.js, play.css, game.js, game_bg.wasm, or any of the five generated GLBs, that contains a root-absolute URL, or that leaks a build host path into the generated bindings.

challenges.title: Every generated surface rendered far brighter than the typed cel-shift palette
challenges.impact: The first real screenshots looked washed out and no frame could ever have met the visual contracts: ink measured 0.07 percent of the frame against a mandatory 3 percent floor, rack shadow measured 0.05 percent, and mean linear luminance sat at 0.743 against a ceiling of 0.572. The cause was invisible from the source data, because the RON palette roles, the GLB material names, and the committed bytes were all exactly right.
challenges.approach: Sampling the exact rendered colours showed the pattern: white came out white but ink #1F2A33 came out #2F3A43 and teal #2FB8A8 came out #77DDD4, a brightening that only spares saturated whites. That is the signature of an sRGB value being interpreted as linear. glTF defines baseColorFactor in linear space, while the typed palette is sRGB, and the generator was writing the sRGB channels straight through.
challenges.resolution: assetgen now converts each role with LinearRgba::from before writing baseColorFactor, the asset contract asserts the linear value rather than the sRGB one, and every GLB was regenerated. Palette accuracy went from 90 to 98 percent of pixels within RGB distance 24 of an approved role, and the same fix moved ink, rack shadow, hose charcoal, teal, and yellow onto their authored values in one step.

challenges.title: The overhead cable trays hid the technician at two of the four camera headings
challenges.impact: The projected-worker-crop contract found no hard hat and no hi-vis pixels at all in the settled north-west capture and only 0.04 percent in the south-west one. The technician was completely behind a cable tray, which is a real playability failure rather than a measurement artefact: at half the headings the player could not see their own character while standing at a rack.
challenges.approach: An orthographic camera at 57 degrees elevation projects anything at height h onto the ground point cot(57 deg) / sqrt(2) times h away along each ground axis, which is 0.459h per axis. At the original 4 m the trays landed 1.84 m away, right on top of a technician standing at a rack face. Every height was checked against the 6 m rack row spacing rather than nudged.
challenges.resolution: OVERHEAD_TRAY_HEIGHT is now 6.54 m, the height whose 3 m per-axis offset is exactly half the rack row spacing, so a tray hung over an aisle always projects over a rack row and never over the walkway. The trays were also narrowed and their hanging hose runs removed. All fourteen frames now carry hard hat and hi-vis pixels inside the projected worker crop, and the constant carries the derivation beside it so it cannot be tuned away.

challenges.title: The screenshot history links images the build that renders the page never writes
challenges.impact: Site generation validates that every local link resolves to a real file, which is what keeps a published page from shipping a broken image. The visual history breaks that assumption: only the newest accepted point is written by the build that renders the page, and every earlier point is a file the assembly step copies forward from the previous pages-live branch. Rendering the history therefore failed validation, and rendering it without images would have published a history nobody can look at.
challenges.approach: The alternative of passing the whole previous site into the generator was rejected: the generator would then have to trust and copy an arbitrary directory of images, which is exactly the containment the publication rules exist to prevent. Instead the generated site declares what it expects assembly to supply.
challenges.resolution: build_site publishes gallery.json beside index.html, and validate_site_output reads that manifest and accepts a screenshots/history/ link the manifest declares. A history link the manifest does not declare is still a broken link, assemble_site now carries screenshots/history/ forward through a green replacement, and a failed build renders the history without images because it publishes no manifest of its own.

challenges.title: Publishing why a build failed, from a job that stops at its first failure
challenges.impact: The hub exists to show the current commit's real status, and the gate matrix is most valuable exactly when something is red. A workflow step runs its commands under `set -e`, so the first failing gate ends the step and every later gate is never measured: a run whose formatting drifted would publish one red row and say nothing about the tests, the render contract, or the release build. Worse, the obvious fix of marking the whole step `continue-on-error` makes the job report success, and a job that never fails cannot gate the web build or the deployment.
challenges.approach: Two rejected alternatives shaped this. Running each gate as its own workflow step with `continue-on-error` loses the measured duration and forces every result to be reassembled from step outcomes in workflow expressions, which cannot be tested anywhere. Parsing the job log for results was rejected outright: raw command output is exactly what may never reach a public page.
challenges.resolution: scripts/run-gate.sh runs one named gate, measures its wall clock, appends a single line naming the gate, its status, and its duration, and always exits zero, so every later gate still runs. Each job then summarizes those lines into a strict result manifest, uploads the manifest with its evidence in an `if: always()` step, and only afterwards fails once in a verdict step of its own. Publish merges the two manifests, synthesizing skipped and failed rows for a job that produced none, so a job that never uploaded anything publishes the gap it left instead of a silent green.
